Family Health

Hair around the nipples: what is normal?

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A dark or coarse hair around a nipple can be surprising, but a few hairs in the surrounding areola are a normal variation. The useful questions are whether growth is changing quickly, whether other symptoms have appeared and what, if anything, you want to do about it.

A few areolar hairs are a normal variation

Much of the body has hair follicles, including skin around the breasts. Fine, pale hairs can be easy to miss, while a few darker, longer or coarser hairs stand out. What people call nipple hair usually grows in the areola, the darker skin surrounding the nipple, rather than from the milk-duct opening.

The amount and appearance vary between people and can change over time. A few longstanding hairs are not evidence of poor hygiene or an illness, and they do not need to be removed for health reasons. There is no reliable reason to compare yourself with photographs that may show shaved or edited skin. You can choose to leave the hair alone or discuss removal if it bothers you.

Hormones matter, but one hair is not a hormone test

Body hair can change around puberty, pregnancy and menopause, as well as with ordinary aging. Hormonal shifts can influence the thickness and visibility of hair, but there is no specific age in your twenties or thirties when a new areolar hair automatically means a hormonal imbalance.

Androgens, including testosterone, are present in everyone. Higher androgen levels or greater follicle sensitivity to them can produce hirsutism: a broader pattern of coarse, dark hair in areas such as the face, chest, abdomen or back. A few local hairs without other symptoms are different from rapidly increasing hair in several areas.

Pay attention to the pattern and pace of change. Increasing facial or body hair with oily skin, acne, irregular or absent periods, or thinning scalp hair is worth discussing with a clinician. Sudden marked growth, a deepening voice or an unexplained increase in muscle bulk needs prompt assessment rather than cosmetic treatment alone.

Review medicines before assuming a new disorder

Some medicines can alter hair growth, including testosterone or anabolic steroid products, glucocorticoid medicines and particular immune-suppressing treatments such as ciclosporin. Not every medicine in these groups has the same effect, and medicine-related hair growth is not always the same androgen-pattern process as hirsutism.

Bring a list of prescriptions, injections, creams and supplements to an appointment, including when they were started or changed. A prescriber can assess whether the timing fits and whether any change is appropriate. Do not abruptly stop steroid medicines or an immunosuppressant because of a cosmetic concern. The condition they are treating and the risks of withdrawal also need consideration.

PCOS and Cushing’s syndrome need a broader assessment

The condition widely known as polycystic ovary syndrome, or PCOS, is a common cause of androgen-related excess hair. Current NHS information uses the name polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, or PMOS. It can involve irregular ovulation and periods, acne, scalp hair loss and difficulty conceiving. Hair around the nipples by itself cannot diagnose it, and ovarian cysts are not a requirement for every person with the condition.

Cushing’s syndrome is a much less common cause of changes in hair and periods. It involves prolonged excess glucocorticoid exposure, from medicines or excess cortisol produced within the body. Features such as easy bruising, wide purple stretch marks, muscle weakness and changes in fat distribution make a broader clinical assessment more useful than focusing on one coarse hair.

Pituitary tumors can cause excess ACTH, the signal that tells the adrenal glands to make cortisol; this form is called Cushing’s disease. Adrenal tumors or ACTH-producing tumors elsewhere, including the lungs, are other possible causes. The pituitary must not be excluded from the list. These are explanations a clinician considers when the overall pattern fits, not reasons to assume that ordinary areolar hair indicates a tumor.

Choose tests according to the symptoms

A clinician will usually ask when the change began, whether periods are regular, whether pregnancy is possible, what medicines you use and whether similar hair patterns run in the family. They may examine the distribution of hair and look for other signs of a hormone condition. You can also explain how much the hair affects your confidence or comfort.

Blood tests may be useful for wider hirsutism, menstrual changes or other concerning findings. The Endocrine Society advises against routine androgen testing for isolated local unwanted hair when periods are regular and there is no abnormal hirsutism pattern. More tests do not automatically make a normal variation clearer. If testing is needed, the clinician chooses which hormones, timing and follow-up suit the question.

If you want removal, start gently

Leaving the hair alone is a valid option. If you prefer to shorten it, careful trimming avoids pulling out the follicle. Use a clean small tool, good lighting and a position in which you can clearly see the skin. Leave a little clearance instead of trying to cut flush with the areola, and stop if you cannot control the tool safely.

Trimming removes the visible part, so the hair will grow again and may need repeating. It does not treat a hormone disorder, but it can be enough for a few bothersome hairs. Do not cut into a raised bump or mistake the normal small glands on the areola for ingrown hairs. Seek advice first if the area is sore, cracked or inflamed.

Plucking, shaving and waxing can damage sensitive skin

Tweezers remove a hair from the follicle, but pulling can cause pain, irritation, ingrown hair or infection. A warm shower may soften skin and hair; it does not literally open pores or make plucking risk-free. Breast-specific NHS advice favors careful trimming over plucking or shaving around the nipple.

A razor can nick the nipple or areola, and regrowth may irritate the skin or become ingrown. Waxing or an epilator pulls multiple hairs and may also cause irritation, skin injury or burns from hot wax. A salon appointment does not automatically make those methods suitable for the nipple area. Discuss safer options if the skin is sensitive or you are uncertain.

Do not repeatedly squeeze or dig at an ingrown hair. Increasing redness, warmth, swelling, pain or pus can indicate an infection; seek advice, particularly if you feel unwell or have fever. During breastfeeding, avoid creating sore or broken skin where the baby feeds and ask for help if pain interferes with feeding.

Creams and home light devices have area restrictions

Depilatory creams work by breaking down hair, but can irritate or burn delicate skin. A product suitable for legs, underarms or the bikini line should not be assumed safe on nipples or areolas. Avoid using it there and follow all restrictions rather than trying a stronger product when a gentler one has not worked.

The same caution applies to home laser or intense pulsed light devices. Follow the manufacturer’s prohibited-area and skin-tone instructions, including any direction to avoid the nipple and areola. A patch test somewhere else does not establish safety for this pigmented, sensitive area. Do not use a device over a wound or inflamed skin.

Professional removal has benefits and limits

Laser treatment targets pigment in hair and can reduce growth over a series of sessions. Its suitability depends on the hair, skin tone, treatment area and device. The pigmented areola needs particular care; a dermatologist should assess the exact location rather than assuming a treatment used on the legs is suitable around the nipple.

Electrolysis treats individual follicles with electrical energy and can be useful for hairs that do not respond well to laser, including lighter hairs. Both methods can be uncomfortable and require repeated appointments, with costs that add up. Ask about the practitioner’s qualifications, likely number of visits, aftercare and the realistic chance of regrowth.

Laser can cause burns, blisters, pigment changes or scarring, particularly in inexperienced hands. Maintenance may be needed even after a successful course. Neither a single session nor a package price guarantees permanent removal of every hair. Tell the clinician if you are pregnant, breastfeeding or taking medicines that affect the skin before booking treatment.

Treat an underlying cause when treatment is needed

Hormone-related hirsutism may be treated with medicines as well as hair removal. For many people who are not trying to conceive, a combined contraceptive pill is one possible starting option. It contains estrogen and a progestogen, but it is not suitable for everyone. The clinician considers health conditions, clot risk, pregnancy plans and the reason for treatment.

An antiandrogen may sometimes be added or selected in appropriate circumstances. These medicines can affect fetal development and require an appropriate pregnancy-prevention plan when pregnancy is possible. An unspecified single-hormone tablet is not interchangeable with a treatment chosen for hirsutism. Do not take someone else’s prescription or self-treat a few hairs with hormones.

Hair changes improve gradually, often over several months. Medicines do not instantly remove existing hairs, and a few stable areolar hairs may need no medical treatment at all. Arrange a separate assessment for a new breast lump, unexplained nipple discharge, persistent nipple rash or new inversion; those findings should not be explained away by the presence of hair.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Isolated local hair and widespread or rapidly progressing hirsutism need different assessments.

Sensitive nipple and areolar skin needs more caution than general body-hair removal advice suggests.

How BeMama can help

Note the timing of changes, menstrual symptoms and medicine use before an appointment. You can ask about cosmetic options without assuming a hormone disorder.

When to seek help

Seek prompt assessment for sudden coarse hair growth with a deepening voice or muscle change. Fever or worsening redness, swelling or pus after removal needs medical advice; new breast lumps, discharge or persistent skin changes need separate assessment.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • A few longstanding areolar hairs are usually normal and removal is optional.
  • The speed and distribution of growth matter more than one hair.
  • Medicines and hormone conditions can contribute, but testing is selective.
  • Careful trimming is a gentler option than pulling at the follicle.
  • Professional and prescription treatments need individualized advice and pregnancy precautions.

Frequently asked questions

Is hair around the nipple normal?

Yes. Hair follicles can be present in the areola, and a few stable hairs are a normal variation. They do not mean poor hygiene.

Does nipple hair prove I have PCOS?

No. PCOS, also called PMOS in current NHS guidance, is assessed from a wider pattern of symptoms and findings. One or several local hairs cannot diagnose it.

Does everyone need a hormone blood test?

No. Isolated local hair with regular periods and no wider concerning pattern often does not need androgen testing. Your clinician selects tests based on the overall picture.

Can a medicine make body hair grow more?

Yes. Some hormone, steroid and immune-suppressing medicines can do this. Review the medicine with its prescriber instead of stopping it yourself.

Can a pituitary problem cause Cushing’s syndrome?

Yes. An ACTH-producing pituitary tumor can cause excess cortisol; that form is called Cushing’s disease. Ordinary areolar hair alone is not evidence of it.

What is a gentle way to shorten a few hairs?

Careful trimming with a clean tool, good lighting and clearance from the skin is an option. Leaving the hair alone is also fine.

Does a warm shower make plucking safe?

No. Warm water does not open pores or remove the risks of irritation, ingrown hair or infection. Breast-specific guidance favors careful trimming.

Can I use a leg-hair removal cream on the areola?

Do not assume it is suitable. These products can irritate or burn sensitive skin; avoid application to nipples and areolas and follow the product restrictions.

Will one laser session permanently remove the hair?

No. Results vary, several sessions may be needed and regrowth can occur. The exact area and skin tone need professional assessment.

Can I take antiandrogens while trying to conceive?

Do not self-treat. Antiandrogens can affect fetal development and require appropriate pregnancy precautions. Discuss fertility plans before choosing treatment.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
